title: Before the breakup (Sn 4.10)
hookLine: read it: the one at peace before the body breaks
tomorrow: where do quarrels actually start? the next poem follows the trail.

lines: THE SAME ON HER WORST DAY.
cards: At a memorial, someone stands up to talk about a grandmother. She never once gossiped. I never saw her in a hurry.
She was the same on her worst day as on her best. Nobody mentions a job title. The tenth poem of the chapter of eights is built the same way.
Someone asks the Buddha: how does a person see, and how do they live, to be called at peace? And the answer comes back as a portrait.

teach.b: One question today: what does peace look like in a person? In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata: free of craving before the body breaks up, not leaning on the past, nothing pushed ahead into the future.

teach.h: NO ANGER, NO FEAR, NO HURRY.
teach.b: Without anger, without fear, not boasting, not anxious, speaking with thought, not restless. Not grieving what's gone. Not envious, not stingy, not cutting, not spreading gossip.
Gentle. Not thrown when there's no gain. And not counting himself equal, better or lower than anyone.
That one, the poem says, is called at peace. Notice it's ordinary. No visions.
Habits of the tongue and the heart. Now a neighbor who says something close.
In the New Testament, Paul writes to the Philippians, in the King James Version: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."
Shared: peace is learned, and it holds in any state, plenty or want. And an honest difference. Paul goes on to say his strength comes through Christ.
The poem's sage leans on nothing outside, not even a view.
Two portraits, side by side, alike in a real way, different in what holds them up.
Neither needs the other to be the same.

how: Buddhist teachers read portraits like this one as a description of the awakened sage and as a mirror for ordinary practice; Christians read Paul's letter to the Philippians in church and in private prayer.

o: before a friendship or a romance ends
before a monk leaves the monastery
before the body breaks up at death

games.q: the portrait, and its neighbor — tap the pairs.

s: the poem's person at peace feels nothing at all
the portrait is gentle, thoughtful, unhurried: habits of the tongue and heart, not numbness.
Paul writes that he has learned to be content in any state
Philippians 4:11: in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Paul and the poem say exactly the same thing
both picture learned contentment; Paul's strength comes through Christ, while the sage leans on nothing outside.

games.q: the night before a big exam you're replaying last week's bad grade and dreading next week's. which line of the portrait fits?
o: not grieving the past, nothing pushed ahead into the future.
never feeling fear, because a sage feels nothing at all.
push through tonight; peace is for after the exam is over.
games.why: the portrait doesn't promise numbness. it describes someone not leaning on the past or pushing into the future, which is exactly where the exam worry lives.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you've known who seemed at peace: a grandparent, a neighbor, a coach. Find one trait from today's portrait in them, unhurried, no gossip, the same on a bad day.
Breathe with that one trait, as if you were trying it on.

wordCard.voice: Before the breakup: before the body breaks up at death. The poem's portrait of someone already at peace while there's still time.

orig.note: Pali: at peace, calmed. The poem ends by calling such a person santa, at peace.

carryVoice: Your line: before the end. Peace is a portrait you can start painting now. Poem ten, read.

sources.q: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

sources.ref: Philippians 4:12-13 (content in plenty and in want; strength through Christ)
